questions.q: When we use a database, what does the database manager do?
options: It designs the tables for us
It is a program that manipulates the database for us
It stores a backup copy of the data
questions.explain: Queries are sent to a database manager — a program that manipulates the database on our behalf.
questions.evidence: a program that manipulates the database for us

questions.q: Records in a table are not stored in any particular order. How do you show them in a specific order?
options: Specify the order explicitly with ORDER BY
Rows always come back in the order they were inserted
questions.explain: Ordering is never implicit: you must ask for it with ORDER BY.
questions.evidence: if we want to display them in some order, we must specify that explicitly with ORDER BY

questions.q: Which clause specifies the conditions a record must meet to be included in a query's results?
questions.explain: WHERE filters records; SELECT then decides which columns to show.
questions.evidence: Use WHERE to specify conditions that records must meet in order to be included in a query's results.

questions.q: Which keyword combines the results of two or more queries into one result set?
questions.explain: UNION stacks the results of several queries; JOIN combines columns from several tables.
questions.evidence: Use UNION to combine the results of two or more queries.

questions.q: A record's test in WHERE evaluates to null. What happens to that record?
options: The query stops with an error
It is left out — WHERE keeps only records for which the test is true
questions.explain: Null is neither true nor false, and WHERE keeps only rows whose test is true.
questions.evidence: the only records kept by a WHERE are those for which the test is true

questions.q: If you add two values and one of them is null, what is the result?
questions.explain: Null means 'unknown', so arithmetic with it is unknown too.
questions.evidence: If we add two values, and one of them is null, the result is null.

questions.q: What is a primary key?
options: A value, or combination of values, that uniquely identifies each record in a table
A value from one table that identifies a record in another table
The first column of every table
A password that protects the database
questions.explain: A primary key identifies each record uniquely; a foreign key points at another table's records.
questions.evidence: A primary key is a value, or combination of values, that uniquely identifies each record in a table.

questions.q: A value from one table that identifies a unique record in another table is called a…
questions.explain: Foreign keys are what joins match on.
questions.evidence: A foreign key is a value (or combination of values) from one table that identifies a unique record in another table.

questions.q: Why should every value in a database be atomic?
options: So a value doesn't contain parts we might want to work with separately
Atomic values use less disk space
Because SQL cannot store long text
questions.explain: Store parts separately (for example family and personal names) instead of splitting strings later.
questions.evidence: not contain parts that we might want to work with separately

questions.q: According to the lesson, when is it simpler and safer to modify data?
options: When the table has no columns
When you have just deleted the table
When every record has a unique primary key
questions.explain: A unique key lets you target exactly the record you mean to change or delete.
questions.evidence: It is simpler and safer to modify data when every record has a unique primary key.

questions.q: What does SQL stand for?
questions.explain: Queries are written in SQL and sent to a database manager.
questions.evidence: Queries are written in a language called SQL , which stands for "Structured Query Language"

questions.q: Can data be moved from one database manager to another?
options: No, data is locked to one system
Yes — managers can import and export formats such as CSV and SQL
questions.explain: Each manager stores data differently, but common formats bridge them.
questions.evidence: every database manager can import and export data in a variety of formats like .csv, SQL, so it is possible to move information from one to another

questions.q: What is a relational database?
options: A way to store and manipulate information in tables
questions.explain: Tables hold records; records have fields.
questions.evidence: A relational database is a way to store and manipulate information.

questions.q: Why do queries often return redundant information?
options: Because SQL repeats every row twice
Because the data itself is often redundant
Because databases can't store unique values
questions.explain: DISTINCT removes duplicate rows from results.
questions.evidence: Data is often redundant, so queries often return redundant information.

questions.q: How can you get quick turnaround while building a complex query?
options: Run it against a subset of data or a small database of synthetic records
Run it on the full production database each time
Write the whole query at once without testing
questions.explain: Most people 'grow' queries step by step and check each result.
questions.evidence: The best way to achieve a quick turnaround is often to put a subset of data in a temporary database and run our queries against that, or to fill a small database with synthesized records.

questions.q: What does the lesson call one of the most powerful features of a database?
options: Filtering data to select only records that match criteria
questions.explain: WHERE is the clause that does the filtering.
questions.evidence: One of the most powerful features of a database is the ability to filter data

questions.q: What does the lesson say about the completeness of real-world data?
options: It is never complete — there are always holes
Gaps only appear in text fields
questions.explain: Databases represent missing values with null.
questions.evidence: Real-world data is never complete --- there are always holes.

questions.q: Does count include NULL values?
options: No — NULL values are not counted
questions.explain: Counting a column with a NULL gives a smaller number.
questions.evidence: note that any NULL value will not be counted

questions.q: When the database must aggregate a field but isn't told how, what does it do?
options: It picks an actual value from the input set — possibly any of them
It returns an error every time
questions.explain: It might use the first value, the last, or something else.
questions.evidence: when it has to aggregate a field, but isn't told how to, the database manager chooses an actual value from the input set

questions.q: What is another way to describe a foreign key?
options: A key from a foreign country
The last column in a table
The primary key of one table appearing in another table
questions.explain: Foreign keys make joins between tables possible.
questions.evidence: a foreign key is the primary key of one table that appears in some other table

questions.q: Why did the expedition example need a join?
options: The needed data was split across the Site, Visited and Survey tables
The data was in a spreadsheet
questions.explain: Joins combine related records from several tables.
questions.evidence: our latitudes and longitudes are in the Site table, while the dates of measurements are in the Visited table and the readings themselves are in the Survey table

questions.q: Why store personal and family names in separate columns?
options: Splitting full names on spaces is unreliable
questions.explain: Names like 'Eloise St. Cyr' break simple splitting.
questions.evidence: we store the two parts of the name separately because splitting on spaces is unreliable

questions.q: What is the second rule of data hygiene?
options: Every record should have a unique primary key
Every table should have ten columns
questions.explain: The first rule is that every value should be atomic.
questions.evidence: The second rule is that every record should have a unique primary key.

questions.q: Which SQL commands create and delete tables?
questions.explain: INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE change records.
questions.evidence: Use CREATE and DROP to create and delete tables.

questions.q: To update records, what do you tell the database?
options: Which table, what to change the values to, and under what conditions
questions.explain: Without a condition, every record would be changed.
questions.evidence: we tell the database which table we want to update, what we want to change the values to for any or all of the fields, and under what conditions we should update the values

questions.q: Why can deleting records be tricky?
options: The database must stay internally consistent
questions.explain: Other tables may still refer to the record being deleted.
questions.evidence: Deleting records can be a bit trickier, because we have to ensure that the database remains internally consistent.

questions.q: Why are data types a portability headache across database systems?
options: Systems differ in which types they offer and what they call them
questions.explain: Moving a schema between systems often needs type changes.
questions.evidence: Keeping track of what particular systems do or do not offer, and what names they give different data types, is an unending portability headache.

questions.q: Why are spreadsheets a popular way to store and explore data?
options: They handle billions of rows easily
They need less work to set up and get started
questions.explain: Databases need more setup but scale and enforce structure better.
questions.evidence: Spreadsheets are a popular way to store and explore data because it requires less work to setup and get started.

questions.q: What is a cell in a spreadsheet?
options: The intersection of a row and a column
questions.explain: Columns are labelled with letters and rows with numbers.
questions.evidence: A cell is the intersection of a row and column
